en: The Thirteen-Book Collection of Birth Stories,
Chapter on Mangoes (Ambavagga)
1. The Amba Jātaka “In former times,
O practitioner of the holy life, you took my mango fruits, both small and large.”
“By those very same mantras, O Brahmā, the fruits of the trees no longer appear for you.
“I honor the conjunction of the constellations.”
One does not see the moment, the brief instant,
or the conjunction of the constellations; yet, having obtained the moment and the conjunction of the constellations, one will surely obtain an abundant fruit of the mango.
“He did not previously announce the conjunction of the constellations;
he did not previously predict the hour or the moment.
He himself gathered an abundance of mango fruit.”
Endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor—
O Brahmā, it was indeed through the chanting of mantras that the fruits of the tree appeared before you.
"Today you cannot even recite your own mantra;
what kind of Dhamma is this that has come upon you today?
'The son of a Caṇḍāla gave me [this].'"
He recited the mantras and the natural order according to the Dhamma;
"And do not ask me my name and clan,
lest the hidden meaning of the mantra be lost."
Thus, when questioned by the Lord of Men among the people,
overcome by conceit, I spoke a falsehood:
"These are the mantras of the Brahmin," which was wrong.
"Having lost my wealth, I weep as a pauper.
"Whether it be *eraṇḍa* trees, *pucimanda* trees,
or even *pālibhaddaka* trees;"
One who seeks honey will find it;
for he is the most excellent of trees.
Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and vaiśyas...
Whether they be Śūdras, Caṇḍālas,
or Pukkusas— from whomever one may learn the Dhamma,
he indeed is the supreme person for that individual.
Having inflicted upon him both punishment and death,
seize this wretch by the neck and drag him away—
he who has obtained the supreme goal with such great difficulty!
“Through pride and arrogance, they have brought about their own ruin.
“As one who, while imagining himself equal,
might fall into a pit, a cave, or a hell with fetid feet;”
As one might step on a rope thinking it is a black snake,
or as a blind man might grasp at a flame;
even so, O wise one, you have stumbled over me.
“Your counsel has been given up, yet it blazes up again and again.
“I bestowed my counsel upon you in accordance with the Dhamma,
and you too accepted it in accordance with the Dhamma.”
I myself, being well-pleased, made this aspiration:
"May no spell abandon one who stands firm in the Dhamma.
O fool, even a spell obtained with great difficulty—
That which is so difficult to obtain today in the world of men—
though having obtained it,
one of little wisdom has brought it to ruin by speaking falsehoods.
To one who is foolish, deluded, ungrateful,
speaking falsehoods, and unrestrained—
to such a person we do not give the mantras.
“Whence have you come, O wise one? You do not please me.
Thus ends the first Amba Jātaka.
